title: Why does a naive save() loop for bulk inserts balloon memory? How does the flush+clear-every-N-rows pattern fix it?
shortTitle: What is the batch insert flush+clear pattern?

s1_definition.profdef: A naive loop that calls `save()` for each of many entities inside one transaction accumulates every entity in the persistence context, along with a dirty-checking snapshot for each, so memory grows linearly with row count and eventually triggers `OutOfMemoryError`. The fix is the **flush+clear pattern**: process a fixed batch of N rows, call `flush()` to push their SQL to the database, then `clear()` to detach them and free their memory, and repeat. This keeps the context size bounded to N regardless of total rows. It is usually combined with JDBC batching configuration so the flushed inserts also go out efficiently.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk entering a million new account forms. The naive way is to spread all one million forms across their desk at once, keeping a carbon copy of each for checking — the desk (and the whole office) overflows. The flush+clear way is to work in stacks of fifty: fill in fifty forms, hand them to the vault for processing (flush), then clear those fifty and their carbons off the desk (clear) before starting the next fifty. The desk never holds more than fifty forms, so the office never overflows no matter how many million forms there are.
s1_definition.oneliner: A naive save() loop keeps every entity and snapshot in the context (memory grows to OOM); flush+clear every N rows bounds the context size and keeps memory flat.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A naive loop that calls `save()` for each of many entities inside one transaction accumulates every entity in the persistence context, along with a dirty-checking snapshot for each, so memory grows linearly with row count and eventually triggers `OutOfMemoryError`. The fix is the **flush+clear pattern**: process a fixed batch of N rows, call `flush()` to push their SQL to the database, then `clear()` to detach them and free their memory, and repeat. This keeps the context size bounded to N regardless of total rows. It is usually combined with JDBC batching configuration so the flushed inserts also go out efficiently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk entering a million new account forms. The naive way is to spread all one million forms across their desk at once, keeping a carbon copy of each for checking — the desk (and the whole office) overflows. The flush+clear way is to work in stacks of fifty: fill in fifty forms, hand them to the vault for processing (flush), then clear those fifty and their carbons off the desk (clear) before starting the next fifty. The desk never holds more than fifty forms, so the office never overflows no matter how many million forms there are.

**One line to remember:** A naive save() loop keeps every entity and snapshot in the context (memory grows to OOM); flush+clear every N rows bounds the context size and keeps memory flat.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — importing a million-row customer file crashed the service.** At National Bank of India, a nightly import of new accounts from a partner file loaded all rows in one transaction with a save loop, and the service died with OutOfMemoryError around 400,000 rows. This is exactly the unbounded-context problem.

**Problem 2 — even after fixing memory, the inserts were slow.** Once memory was controlled, the inserts still ran one round trip each because batching was not configured and the id used IDENTITY. This is exactly why flush+clear is paired with JDBC batch config and SEQUENCE ids.

What the code will do: a `BulkImportService` with a naive method (explained as the anti-pattern) and the correct flush+clear batch method, with the entity using SEQUENCE ids and the config enabling JDBC batching.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: one million account names, batch size 100, heap capped at 256 MB.

Step 1 — the loop persists accounts. Each persist makes the entity managed, assigns an id from the pre-fetched sequence pool, and queues an insert. No SQL yet.

Step 2 — after 100 persists, `flush()` sends those 100 inserts to the database as one JDBC batch (because batch_size is 100 and ids come from a sequence, batching works).

Step 3 — `clear()` detaches all 100 entities, dropping references and snapshots so the garbage collector reclaims them. The context is empty again.

Step 4 — the loop continues. Because each batch is flushed and cleared, the resident set stays around 100 entities, so heap usage oscillates in a narrow band instead of climbing. With the naive loop, heap would climb past 256 MB and the JVM would throw OutOfMemoryError well before a million rows.

Step 5 — a final `flush()` handles the last partial batch, and commit finalizes all one million inserts.

```
2026-10-24 01:21:05 INFO  Imported 100 accounts; context cleared
2026-10-24 01:21:05 INFO  Imported 200 accounts; context cleared
2026-10-24 01:23:40 INFO  Bulk import complete: 1000000 accounts (memory stayed flat)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  batchImport(1,000,000 names)   heap capped 256MB
    │
    ▼
  LOOP
    │  persist(new Account) → MANAGED + INSERT queued (id from seq pool)
    │
    ├─ every 100 ──→ flush()  → one JDBC batch of 100 INSERTs → DB
    │               clear()  → detach 100 → GC frees them
    │               context: 100 → 0   heap: sawtooth (flat)
    ▼
  final flush() → last partial batch → COMMIT
  ── Naive variant ──
  persist × 1,000,000 with NO clear → context holds all → heap climbs → OOM @ ~400k
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Batch Insert flush+clear (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Chunk processing: persist N → flush → clear → repeat       │
  │  Unit of Work with bounded context                          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: service imports; EntityManager manages the context      │
  │  O: tune BATCH / id strategy via config, not code rewrites  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Memory Model (as prose) ──
  Naive : context = all N entities + N snapshots → O(N) heap → OOM.
  flush+clear: context ≤ BATCH → O(BATCH) heap → flat sawtooth.

  ── State Diagram: entity in batch ──
  [TRANSIENT] ─persist─▶ [MANAGED, queued] ─flush─▶ [IN-DB] ─clear─▶ [DETACHED→GC]

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. loop persist (id from seq pool)
  2. every 100 → flush (JDBC batch) → clear (free heap)
  3. final flush → commit

  (Caution) IDENTITY ids disable batching. (Caution) one big TX = huge rollback risk;
     consider per-batch transactions for very large loads.
  Rule: bound the context with flush+clear; pair with batch_size + SEQUENCE ids.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A naive bulk insert loop that calls save for each entity inside one transaction balloons memory because the persistence context holds a strong reference to every managed entity and a dirty-checking snapshot for each one, and because the transaction stays open, nothing is ever released. For a million rows I am holding a million objects and a million snapshots, so the heap climbs until the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError, and as a secondary effect dirty checking gets slower because each flush has to scan an ever-larger context.

The fix is the flush and clear pattern. I process a fixed batch of rows, call flush to push that batch's inserts to the database, then call clear to detach every managed entity so the garbage collector can reclaim it, and I repeat. After each clear the context is empty, so the resident set stays bounded to the batch size regardless of how many total rows I am importing, and memory oscillates in a narrow band instead of climbing. I always add a final flush for the last partial batch.

At National Bank of India our nightly import of new accounts from a partner file used to crash with an OutOfMemoryError around four hundred thousand rows because it loaded everything in one save loop. I rewrote it to persist in batches of a hundred and flush then clear after each batch, and on a capped heap it then imported a million rows with flat memory. But flush and clear only solves memory, so I also configured JDBC batching by setting the batch size, enabling ordered inserts, and switching the id generation from identity to a sequence with a matching allocation size, because identity generation forces an immediate insert per row and disables batching entirely. The nuances I always mention are that the whole loop is still one transaction, so a failure rolls back everything and holds locks a long time, which is why for very large loads I sometimes commit per batch to bound the rollback and lock window, accepting that partial progress persists, and that after a clear any entity reference I kept is detached so I must not touch its lazy associations.

---

keyPoints: Naive save() loop: all entities in persistence context — OOM for 100K rows
Fix: flush + clear every N rows (e.g., every 50)
for (i=0; i<items.size(); i++) { save(item); if (i%50==0) { flush(); clear(); } }
